title: WHACC Method
text: Students in many health science programs, especially in nursing and pharmacy programs, often struggle with dosage calculations and related problems. While many methods exist (desired/have, proportional reasoning, dimensional analysis), dimensional analysis is often suggested as the most powerful and recommended by these programs. And, while dimensional analysis is by far the most robust method, many students still struggle with using it correctly. Students often struggle with identifying their target in setting up dimensional analysis problems, identifying irrelevant information, parsing the problem itself, and losing track of units. I developed the WHACC method to attempt to mitigate these issues.

title: WHACC Method
WHACC Method
text:
Design rationale
The WHACC method was designed to address common problem I observed when working with students on these sorts of problems. The most common issues encountered were

not knowing when to stop/including irrelevant information,
not knowing how to begin, and
losing track of calculations.

Beginning each problem by identifying the Want, as well as the constant repetition of “Do I have what I want yet?” after each step in the Align and Cancel cycle, are meant to keep the student focused on the units and give them a clear sign for when they can move on. By beginning the very first Align step with, not an arbitrary choice of starting point but a careful selection of a factor with a desired unit, the student is locked into a solution process that (most of the time) produces the correct answer.
The Want and the Have steps also give the student a relatively simple task to start with while breaking down the problem from a potentially dense paragraph to a simple list of relevant information. This allows the student to immediately put pen to paper without having to worry about parsing the paragraph itself in one go. By requiring the student to write down all numbers and units in the Have step, they can also save any worrying about relevant vs. irrelevant information for the dimensional analysis step itself, where that sort of determination often falls out naturally by just paying attention to the units.
The final calculate step also forces the student to avoid juggling calculations throughout the problem. It’s very easy to drop or repeat steps by accident when the student is doing the calculations piecemeal, and this is a common source of “silly” mistake. In settings like nursing school, where no partial credit is given, we want to make the process as smooth as possible, with as many guiderails as possible. Saving all the calculations for the end, after the units can all be cancelled out and compared to the desired units, gives a powerful tool for students to catch these sorts of silly errors. Likewise, only having a single calculator use reduces the potential for transcription errors to a minimum.
I’ve also found this method to be very useful in reducing cognitive load. For many problems, the solution can be found by a rote application of the WHACC method, and the student never has to make a single active decision. The Want and Have steps reduce the amount of rereading the student has to do from the problem paragraph. Starting with a unit that matches a unit the student Wants gives a clear starting point for dimensional analysis, and the Calculate step minimizes the number of awkward switches between pen and paper (or marker and whiteboard) and calculator, which can be useful for stressed, frustrated, or distracted students during exams.

title: WHACC Method
text:
Reflection
I am very happy with the WHACC method, and I’ve found it to be very useful in getting students comfortable with dimensional analysis. Dimensional analysis as applied to these sorts of problem often stops being a math problem and becomes more of a jigsaw puzzle, where the student is merely flipping fractions one way or another to line up the units in the appropriate way. Using the WHACC method, I’ve consistently seen students shift from trying to work out a long and complicated math problem to a straightforward spatial reasoning approach, where their only concern is whether or not they want a particular unit on top of the fraction or on bottom.
That being said, the WHACC method still occasionally requires some active judgement from students. In particular, problems where there are repeated units among the Haves might require a student to select which repetition is the relevant one. For example, we might consider the problem

The doctor orders a patient be given 60 mg of Drug C every 4 hours. The package insert for Drug C gives a range of 5-15 mg/kg/day. Drug C is available in a concentration of 10mg/ml, and the patient’s weight is 44 pounds. Is this a safe dosage?

If we follow through on the WHACC method, we inevitably wind up with






NoteWHACC: Align




The doctor orders a patient be given 60 mg of Drug C every 4 hours. The package insert for Drug C gives a range of 5-15 mg/kg/day. Drug C is available in a concentration of 10mg/ml, and the patient’s weight is 44 pounds. Is this a safe dosage?

Want: \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{dose}}
Have: \frac{60 \text{ mg}}{\text{dose}}, \frac{1 \text{ dose}}{4 \text{ hr}}, \frac{5\text{–}15 \text{ mg}}{\text{kg} \cdot \text{day}}, \frac{10 \text{ mg}}{\text{mL}}, 44 \text{ lb}
Align: x \ \frac{\text{mg}}{\text{dose}} = \ ?


Here, the student has to choose between \frac{60 \text{ mg}}{4 \text{ hr}}, \frac{5\text{–}15 \text{ mg}}{\text{kg} \cdot \text{day}}, and \frac{10 \text{ mg}}{\text{mL}}, and the WHACC method requires some additional rules to make that clear. (In this case, I normally teach the student to decide between the package label and the order by looking at the language used by the question. Phrases like “will be administered”, “to be infused”, “to be given” refer to what you are ordered to do, so you start with the order. “Safe dosage” on the other hand, refers to general guidelines, which you get from the package insert.)

title: Statistical Analysis Trainer
text:
It can be difficult to learn a new technology, particularly one involved with finicky technical work such as statistics. AI, when properly used, can be immensely valuable in helping a student learn a new technology, and is able smooth the learning process out, helping to break down syntax, decode error messages, and identify coding bugs. This particular project was born from a self-study strategy I used personally to get a handle on the statistical language R, as well as adapting my workflow to more appropiately address the needs of students.
For students learning a new language, we want a workflow that enables students to learn independently, while keeping the responsibility for learning firmly on the student’s shoulders.

title: Statistical Analysis Trainer
text:
Design rationale
For new students learning game design and attempting to create their own games, a common adage is “finish a game as quickly as possible”. It’s important for a new learner to see all stages of game design to gain a better understanding of game design as a holistic process. When learning a new statistical langauge and learning how to perform a statistical analysis, it is useful to use a similar approach, and this trainer is an attempt to build a workflow to get a student producing a minimum viable statistical analysis in their language of choice as quickly as possible and then checking the quality of that analysis against a vetted reference analysis.
Following principles of good design, we divide the workflow into two distinct stages, a planning stage and a reveal stage. Each stage begins with a new AI instance and has its own dedicated AI orientation documents and student briefs. The planning stage AI recieves its orientation document, the experimental design description, and the dataset. The reveal stage AI receives its own orientation document, the experimental design description, the dataset, as well as the solution key and the student’s statistical report. This way each stage is kept independent, and the planning AI is unable to easily give away any information to the student. This was a common problem I encountered in my initial experiments with this workflow: an AI would be instructed not to reveal any information about the intended analysis, and then do something like name the dataset “logistic-regression-data.csv”.
While initial experimentation had the AI generate the datasets and the experimental design descriptions on the spot (and it did surprisingly well at this), we found that this had the potential for subtle errors. For example, one analysis examined generated data about patient recovery after different types of heart surgeries. In this scenario, the variable length_of_stay measured the number of days post-surgery the patient stayed at the hospital, and this variable was intended to be correlated to the type of surgery. When the data was generated, however, this correlation was not implemented, which lead to a difference between the intended analysis and the actual data. Since these sorts of errors are hidden in sets of data, they can be difficult to spot, and so we avoid this problem by pre-generating and testing experimental design descriptions and datasets to ensure accuracy.
Each pregenerated dataset comes with a chance of having a potential complication in the data that the student must account for. The current list of possible complications is violations of assumptions, underpowered true effects, aliased variables, outcome-dependent variables, post-treatment variables, confounding variables, and unbalanced groups. This is an intential design choice to force the student to diligently check their assumptions and variables. Currently, zero to one complications are chosen when generating each dataset, and these complications are checked to make sure they measurably distort the outcomes of the analysis if not correctly handled with the exception of underpowered true effects. For underpowered true effects, these complications are not meant to distort the analysis, but to impress on the student that even a correct analysis can miss true effects due to random chance in sampling or underpowered experiments.

text:
Showcase
We provide an example showcase of what this learning experience might look like with a student. We show the uploaded materials for both stages, a transcript of the chat logs for both stages, and the two drafts of the student’s report.

Stage 1

Student briefAI orientationExperimental descriptionDatasetAI/Student chat log



This is an exercise in using an AI workflow to engage in statistical analysis of a pre-generated experiment and dataset. Your role will be to review the experimental design description and dataset, decide on the appropriate statistical tests to run, analyze the data using your statistical software of choice, and then write up a brief report presenting your statistical analysis. The goal is to give you a beginning-to-end experience of doing a statistical analysis. This exercise works in two stages, with two sets of folders marked stage 1 and stage 2. In stage 1, you will upload the content of the stage 1 folder (ai-orientation-1.md, data.csv, experimental-description.md) to your AI of choice. The AI’s role is to provide with assistance running the tests and writing the report. The AI should help with using the statistical software, enabling you to run your chosen tests, interpreting errors and outputs. The AI should not help you with making decisions about which methods are appropriate, analyzing the dataset, or hinting towards the correct answer.
For stage 1, you will upload the appropriate documents and then review experimental-description.md and data.csv. From the design description, you will choose the appropriate method to analyze the data. You will then decide on which variables, if any, should be excluded from the analysis for design reasons. You will then check that the relevant statistical assumptions are met for your chosen method, note any existing complications in the data, fit the model using your statistical software of choice, and then write the report. The report should include

the design,
your chosen method of analysis with justification,
a decision to include or exclude for each variable with justification,
checks of the relevant assumptions for your chosen method,
results with effect sizes and confidence intervals, and
interpretation of those results with respect to the initial experimental design.

Once the report is written, you should upload the report and the contents of the stage 2 folder (solution-key.md, experimental-description.md, data.csv, ai-orientation-2.md) to a new AI instance. This is to avoid prior discussion with the first AI instance from influencing the analysis of your report. Once the report is uploaded, the new AI instance will evaluate your report against the solution key. The AI will provide some hints as to errors in the analysis, if any exist, and then give you one opportunity to find and revise the errors. If revision is necessary, make the revisions and reupload the revised report. The AI will then reveal the contents of the solution key, included which variables should have been excluded, what complications existed in the data (if any), the results of the statistical tests and model fitting, and the intended interpretation of those results.
This project is expected to be completed in 20-60 minutes depending on your fluency with statistical analysis and your chosen statistical software. While you have access to the solution key in order to upload it to the AI in stage 2, you are strongly encouraged not to look at it before it is revealed at the end of the exercise.




You are an AI assistant helping a student learn to write a minimal statistical analysis. The goal is for a student to be presented with a short experimental design description and a dataset and then write up a complete statistical analysis on the dataset. This dataset may have complications included, such as violations of assumptions, underpowered true effects, aliased variables, outcome-dependent variables, post-treatment variables, confounding variables, and unbalanced groups, so the student will have to check for common complications to ensure their analysis is correct. Your role is to assist the student in this learning experiment without giving away hints to the true solution. Once the report is written, the student will move on to stage 2. For stage 2, the student will upload their report to a new, fresh AI instance, along with a pre-generated key and a new orientation document. This other AI instance will engage in a revision round with the student and then present the answer key, any included complications, and the true effects used to generate the data. The entire analysis is intended to be completed in a single sitting of approximately 20-60 minutes, depending on the student’s familiarity with their software of choice and the statistical analysis. The report should include

the design,
your chosen method of analysis with justification,
a decision to include or exclude for each variable with justification,
checks of the relevant assumptions for your chosen method,
results with effect sizes and confidence intervals, and
interpretation of those results with respect to the initial experimental design.

The student might be working on this independently or as part of a course on statistics. The student might be generally unfamiliar with their statistical software of choice or with statistics more broadly. Your role is to assist the student with syntax and functions, error messages and debugging, how to run a method that the student has chosen, and explaining what a piece of output means if asked. You should not choose the method, choose which variables to include or exclude, write the report’s prose or interpretation, or run the analysis for them.
You have not been given an answer key. This is an intentional design choice to prevent you from inadvertently providing this information to the student. At no point should you attempt to retype, regenerate, summarize, or analyze the dataset on your own. At no point should you attempt to provide a “right answer” or hint at potential complications in the data. Instead, you must work only from the student’s own code and output.
Once an initial draft of the report is complete, tell the student to upload the report, along with the orientation document and solution key in the stage two folder to a fresh instance of AI to move on to the next stage.

TipClaude · turn 3



They’re useful, and two of them you already have through the tidyverse:

dplyr is data wrangling: filter(), select(), mutate() (e.g., converting columns to factors), group_by() + summarise() for group descriptives. It’s loaded automatically by library(tidyverse).
ggplot2 is the plotting system: boxplots, scatterplots, histograms, Q-Q plots. It’s also part of the tidyverse, so it’s loaded automatically too.
ggpubr is not part of the tidyverse. It’s a wrapper around ggplot2 that makes publication-style plots quickly, with functions like ggboxplot(), ggscatter(), ggqqplot(), ggdensity(), and it can add p-values or regression lines to plots. It’s handy if you’d rather not build plots layer by layer.

So in your setup chunk, library(tidyverse) covers dplyr and ggplot2. Just add:
library(ggpubr)
A quick example of each style, so you can see the difference:
ggplot(dat, aes(x = approach, y = qor15_30d)) + geom_boxplot()

ggboxplot(dat, x = "approach", y = "qor15_30d")
Both give the same kind of plot, so use whichever feels more comfortable.

Yes, Knit is how you see the full rendered document, but there are a couple of ways to view things as you go.
1. Run chunks interactively (fastest while working)

Click the green ▶ arrow at the top-right of a chunk, or press Ctrl+Shift+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Enter on Mac), to run that chunk.
Ctrl+Enter runs just the current line or selection.
Output appears right under the chunk in the editor. If you’d rather see it in the Console and Plots pane, click the gear ⚙ next to Knit and choose “Chunk Output in Console.”
Objects you create this way show up in the Environment pane, so later chunks can use them.

2. Knit (the full rendered report)

Click Knit at the top of the editor, or press Ctrl+Shift+K.
This runs the whole document from scratch in a clean session and produces the HTML, PDF, or Word file, which opens in a viewer window or the Viewer pane.
To have it show in the Viewer pane instead of a popup, go to the gear ⚙ → “Preview in Viewer Pane.”

One gotcha: knitting does not use your Environment. If something works when you run chunks interactively but fails on knit, it’s usually because a package is loaded, or a variable is created, somewhere other than in the Rmd itself, or the chunks are out of order. Everything the report needs has to be in the file, top to bottom.
A good rhythm is to run chunks interactively while you’re building and knit every so often to make sure the whole thing still renders cleanly.

Your instinct is right on both counts, and this is a well-studied question.
What randomization actually guarantees
Randomization makes covariates independent of treatment in expectation, over all possible randomizations. Any single realized allocation can be imbalanced by chance. The key point is that this chance imbalance is already accounted for in the inference: p-values and confidence intervals are calibrated over the randomization distribution, which includes the unlucky allocations. So “we had some imbalance by chance, and we proceed” is the textbook-correct stance, not biting a bullet.
Why significance-testing balance is discouraged
Many trials used to report p-values comparing baseline characteristics between arms. CONSORT and most methodologists now advise against this. If randomization was done properly, the null hypothesis is true by construction, so any “significant” difference is by definition a false positive. A descriptive table (means, SDs, percentages) is the recommended way to report balance. Then you judge whether any difference is large enough to matter clinically, not statistically.
How imbalance is handled in practice

Pre-specified covariate adjustment. This is the main tool, and it’s what ANCOVA does. Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates corrects for chance imbalance in them and usually tightens the confidence interval. The important part is choosing covariates in advance, based on prior knowledge of what predicts the outcome, not after looking at which ones came out imbalanced. Choosing adjustment variables based on observed imbalance opens the door to analytic flexibility.
Design-stage fixes, done before allocation:

Stratified (blocked) randomization: randomize separately within strata, e.g., diabetic and non-diabetic patients, so those groups are balanced by design.
Minimization: each new patient is allocated, partly at random, to whichever arm best preserves balance across several factors. It’s common in smaller trials.
Rerandomization: your “hacky” idea is actually a legitimate method (Morgan & Rubin, 2012), if the acceptance rule is specified in advance (e.g., “redraw until the Mahalanobis distance between arms is below threshold a”), and the analysis accounts for the restricted set of allowable allocations. What’s hacky is doing it ad hoc and then analyzing as if it were simple randomization.


Summary: randomize once (or with a pre-specified restriction), report balance descriptively, adjust for pre-specified prognostic covariates, and don’t let the observed balance drive the analysis choices.

title: Pharmaceutical Calculations Flowchart
text: Students in pharmacy programs often struggle with pharmaceutical calculations. While the actual math ability required to solve these problems isn’t deep, many students come into these programs with shaky fundamentals, unprepared for the rigor and pace required by their programs, and ultimately struggle greatly trying to get up to speed with the wide variety of calculation problems on top of all their other work. To try and help these students get up to pace, just-in-time intervention targeting fundamental math skills is often used, and this type of intervention is both good and necessary. However, a solution process-oriented approach to pharmaceutical calculations can be very useful in complementing the standard fundamental skills approach to intervention.

title: Pharmaceutical Calculations Flowchart
text:
The frameworks
Common calculation topics covered in a pharmacy program include

Dosage calculations,
Compounding and recipes,
Weighing accuracy,
Aliquots,
Concentration expressions,
Specific gravity problems,
Single-solution analysis,
Dilution and evaporation,
Alligation,
Reconstitution,
Insulin,
Isotonicity,
Electrolytes,
Pharmacokinetics, and
Patient formulas (Creatinine clearance, body weight, IV to oral conversions, etc.).

Presented like this, this list might seem daunting, but the skills and methods needed to solve these problems have much more overlap than a struggling student might expect. If we sort everything by required math skill, we get:

Plug-and-chug formulas, including

Weighing accuracy,
Dilution and evaporation,
Pharmacokinetics,
Patient formulas,

Dimensional analysis, including

Dosage calculations,
Specific gravity
Isotonicity,
Insulin,
Electrolytes

Proportional reasoning, including

Compounding and recipes,
Aliquots
Concentration expressions,
Single-solution analysis,
Alligation, and
Reconstitution.


The vast majority of pharmaceutical calculation problems can be solved through one of three basic math skills; applying a memorized formula, using dimensional analysis, or using proportional reasoning. Being able to use these three skills fluently is critical for success in any pharmacy program. For some students, though, it might not be sufficient to meet their needs, and a solution process approach can help fill the gaps. I propose the following flowchart.

  C -->|Yes| F["<b>Solve using single-substance methods.</b><div style='text-align:left'>• Concentration expressions<br>• Single-solution analysis<br>• Aliquots</div>"]
  C -->|No| D["<b>Solve using dimensional analysis.</b><div style='text-align:left'>• Dosage calculations <br>• Insulin<br>• Electrolytes<br>• Specific gravity</div>"]




Figure 1: A process-oriented flowchart for pharmaceutical calculations.





This flowchart gives the students a tool to filter problems into different categories based on solution process. Memorized formula or reconsitution of dry powder problems are filtered out first. Reconsitution in particular has a somewhat unique two-prong solution process, where a student must first use the package instructions to calculation the volume of the powdered drug, and then apply that to a proportion to find the answer. The two-step nature of the problem, along with the addition of “hypothetical” information from the package insert of the drug, creates a solution process that doesn’t readily fit into other categories, and students have to learn this type of problem on its own. After that, we filter out multiple combined substances that produce a single total solution, which often requires excellent bookkeeping to solve. The final filter is dimensional analysis methods or single-solution proportion-based methods. There is a great deal of overlap between these two solution processes, and either approach will work for many problems. Due to the relative robustness of dimensional analysis methods, this flowchart takes a maximal approach to which problems are assigned to the dimensional analysis category: if it can be solved with dimensional analysis, students are encouraged to use dimensional analysis over proportional methods. The key question dividing those two categories can be derived by comparing the units of the quantity the problem asks for to the units of the various information given in the problem. If no given information has the exact same units as the desired quantity, dimensional analysis can be used to solve. If a piece of given information does have the exact same units as the desired quantity, then proportional reasoning methods are used.

title: Pharmaceutical Calculations Flowchart
text:
Design rationale
The idea behind this project was to help break down the space of possible pharmaceutical calculation problems along alternative lines to highlight difficulties students face that don’t necessarily relate to an inability to set up a proportion or do dimensional analysis. Ultimately, pharmaceutical calculations are word problems, and any math educator knows that word problems are extradinarily difficult to teach well. They require excellent number sense and mathematical maturity compared to the actual difficulty of the required math, and many pharmacy students come into their programs with shaky math skills that can’t really be addressed by a lecture on ratios and proportions. A solution process approach takes advantage of the fact that the space of common pharmaceutical calculation solutions isn’t that large compared to all possible word problems, and many different problems have similar solution processes. We can lean on those similarities to highlight common strategies that math skill-based approaches might miss.
For example, electrolyte-based problems (problems concerning milliequivalents, milliOsmols, etc.) are often straightforward dimensional analysis problems, but a student might not make that connection, because they’re often taught with a complicated formula. We might also consider an isotonicity problem and an alligation alternate problem.

This project originally started as an attempt to fully characterize pharmaceutical calculations by solution type and math skills. While this was not completely successful, the broad strokes classification used in the flowchart is still useful. In the pharmaceutical calculations practice app, the idea was used to sort problems into broad solution-process categories. To write out the solutions for each problem, solution templates were made up of modular pieces that could be shared between problems with similar solution processes. For example, dimensional analysis problems all use the WHACC method, single-substance problems often use proportions based on concentration or amount of solute/solvent/solution, and multi-substance problems use tables to do the bookkeeping.

title: Welcome!
text: This blog is a place for me to publish my thoughts on education, mathematics, and AI. Expect a lot of stuff on how to use AI well in an educational context, various topics of interest I’ve encountered in my work, especially where it overlaps with math education, and maybe some ramblings about research and other more mathematics-leaning topics I’m interested in.

title: A Gradual Release of Responsibility
text:
In education, there’s a concept, first introduced by David Pearson and Margaret Gallagher, called the gradual release of responsibility (Pearson & Gallagher, 1983). This is a pedagogical method wherein the instructor initially holds all the responsibility for learning, and students are gradually given more and more responsibility until they are learning independently. In a math setting, let’s say, learning how to complete the square to solve quadratic equations, this might look like

The instructor works through an entire problem showing each step of the completing the square algorithm.
The instructor works through another completing the square problem, but this time, they stop before a couple of steps and ask the students what the next step should be.
The instructor works through another problem, and asks the students what comes next for each step.
The instructor gives one more problem, and has the students solve the problem while they observe.
The instructor gives homework to be completed independently.

And so, the responsibility for learning initially rested entirely on the instructor’s shoulders, but more and more responsibility was handed off to the student until they were expected to complete the homework by themselves. This is sometimes referred to as “I do, we do, you do” instruction, first coined by Doug Fisher and Nancy Frey (Fisher & Frey, 2008). While this framework is most commonly applied to instructor/student interactions on a lesson-by-lesson basis, we can zoom out and apply it more broadly to a student’s educational career. A student beginning elementary school is, broadly speaking, engaged in “I do” work. The responsibility for their learning rests entirely with the instructor, and the student has little to no control over their educational experience. For the most part, the student remains in the “I do” stage throughout high school. The student is taking classes required by their school with very little independent choice. They learn to do trigonometry or write an essay by following strict formulas. They read books that are assigned by their teachers. None of this, in a vacuum, is bad. The “I do” stage is very important, both within a single lesson and within education itself. A student has to learn how to learn before they can go out and do it effectively on their own, and we see this progression in undergraduate education. A student slowly picks their major, works through upper level courses, and finally completes a bachelor’s thesis; they work through the “we do” stage, gradually taking more and more responsibility for their own learning. And then when a student progresses to grad school, they’re often in a situation where they’re solely responsible for learning the material.
The key factors that govern this large-scale gradual release of responsibility (GRR) are student motivation and expertise. Without the motivation to actually learn, you can’t trust a student not to seek shortcuts, and without the expertise, you can’t rely on the student to judge whether they’re truly learning effectively. As the student’s expertise grows, they become more able to learn for themselves, and they’re afforded more freedom to focus on subjects they have passion for, increasing their motivation. Alongside this growth, they’re entrusted with more responsibility for their own learning.
This is the framework into which we’re trying to implement AI, and so we must take into account where the responsibility for learning lies when deciding what AI usage is appropriate. With the advent of LLMs, there are three entities that can hold some amount of responsibility for student learning: the instructor, the AI, and the student. Getting the balance right is critical, as many educators have learned.



Takehome midterms grades vs. in-person final grades for Brown University professor Roberto Serrano’s ECON 1170 course. Here, the suspected cause of the grade discrepency is private AI use by students, and not AI implementation by Professor Serrano.


There has obviously been work on this question previously. Perkins, Furze, Roe, and MacVaugh released a paper detailing a descriptive framework of AI usage in educational assessments in 2024 (Perkins, Furze, Roe, & MacVaugh, 2024). Their framework is no AI, AI-assisted idea generation and structuring, AI-assisted editing, AI task completion and human evaluation, and full ai. While this is a solid descriptive framework, it primarily focuses on different levels of independent student usage of AI to complete assignments. It doesn’t supply a guiding principle for the instructor to decide which level is appropriate for their students, and this is the gap I believe a GRR framework can fill.
In lower level courses, which students are often forced to take with little to no input, AI interaction should be extremely restrained. Up through undergraduate introductory or general education courses, AI should mostly be used by the instructor to implement tools they might not be able to do otherwise. Once a student has been able to start a degree path and invest time developing their expertise in their chosen subject, then they should be able to shoulder the burden of more unrestricted AI usage, although it should be with well-defined objectives and limitations. Unrestricted AI usage, insofar as it has anything to do with accredited education, should be limited to students working with a great deal of expertise and motivation. A graduate student researcher, for instance, might well utilize AI in an unrestricted manner to learn new tools, statistical methods, and gain a deeper overview of their field, and this is good AI usage! But it only comes into play when a student is able to take responsibility for their own learning, like we expect for graduate students. Earlier than that, I fear the results of Professor Serrano’s infamous ECON 1170 course are the rule rather than the exception (Whitford, 2026).
I propose the following framework to help differentiate different levels of AI responsibility.

Level 1

    No direct AI/student interaction. All responsibility remains with the instructor.

Level 2

    AI is used to interpret student responses. Almost all responsibility remains with the instructor.

Level 3

    AI is able to reply to student responses within the scope of a well-defined exchange. The instructor defines system prompts for the AI and objective briefings for the student, and the responsibility entrusted to the student and to the AI is determined by the scope of the prompt and the briefing.

Level 4

    AI may be used freely to investigate. The instructor may set an assignment scope, but all remaining responsibility for learning rests with the student.


At level 1, the AI is a nonentity in the learning exchange. If AI is used, it is used solely to develop a tool, and the instructor bears all responsibility for the accuracy and content of this tool. This is where, I believe, the bulk of potential for AI usage lies, letting instructors develop tools that weren’t feasible for them before. My pharmacy calculation practice app is one such example. It was always theoretically possible for me to make this tool, but I never would have found the time to develop it on my own. While AI was used heavily to develop the question bank, I still bear the responsibility to the accuracy of these questions, which I tried to ensure by programmatically generating solutions from problem inputs, checking initial questions by hand, editing solution templates, and continuing to use the tool itself daily so that I can catch other potential problems I missed. The student never actually interacts with the AI.
At level 2, AI can be used to interpret student work, but the AI does not reply to the student. We might consider using AI to identify and sort mistakes in student calculations as an example of a level 2 AI usage. We’ve started to release some responsibility to the AI, but the student experience hasn’t changed from level 1. They’re still doing the same work, and the difference here is how we’re interacting with that work. While I don’t think AI should ever take sole responsibility for grading student work, modern LLMs offer an ability to investigate, interpret, and categorize student work that hasn’t existed. For example, it would be possible to save and scan a semester’s worth of student math work and then analyze the work and sort the errors into conceptual, procedural, and computational errors. This data can then be used to identify pain points in pedagogy or areas of weakness in student prerequisite skills.
Level 3 is where the student and the AI are finally allowed to interact directly. This is the level that every new edtech company under the sun is trying to develop tools for, and this is the level where we must take the most care as educators.



A staged screenshot showing a customer asking a McDonald’s chatbot to write a python program (Goel, 2026).


Here, it’s very easy for a student to overstep the bounds of the assignment, either to disengage with the work altogether or to undercut the desired learning experience of the assignment. Unless you have students that are motivated enough by the material to remain within the guidelines you set for the assignment, you might restrict these assignments to in-class only or require logs of student interactions. Level 3 assignments have a very wide range in how much responsibility rests with the AI. At the lowest level, the interaction might consist of a single prompt and response between the student and AI. At the higher ranges, the interaction might look more like a tutoring session. The statistics analysis trainer is an example of a higher range level 3 interaction. At this level, it is critical to define exactly what your expectations are for both the student and the AI. For the AI, we might craft a strong system prompt that defines the setting of the interaction, the steps and expected student responses at each step, as well as instructions to redirect the student back to the assignment if they start to go outside the boundaries. For the student, we want a similarly strong orientation brief that lays out the exact expectations of the student at each step of the interaction and what the end-product of the interaction should be.
Finally, level 4 is where the student bears total responsibility for their own learning, with the instructor only providing the assignment parameters, and might be best thought of as self-study. My personal attempts to learn R, which led to the aforementioned R analysis session framework, might fall under this category. I started that project because I wanted to learn R for my own benefit, and so I could trust myself not to seek shortcuts. I also had the relevant expertise, having a master’s degree in mathematics, to be able to guide the AI when it started to get hung up on irrelevant points. If a student is not able to handle both, it’s difficult to justify allowing this sort of interaction in an actual course. Insofar as a level 4 assignment might appear in a primary, secondary, or undergraduate curriculum, I can only imagine it working as some sort of low-stakes, participation-only assignment and should otherwise be avoided.
This might seem unnecessarily restrictive to those that view a greater and more transformative role for AI in the classroom. We want to encourage AI fluency, and students will use AI freely in their own time, so we must implement AI widely in education to keep up. I think this misses the point. While AI is poised to make great changes to the field of education, and I believe it has the potential to do so in positive ways, it does not fundamentally change the nature of human learning. It gives educators a new and powerful tool to craft educational experiences that would have been impossible previously, but it does not transform unprepared learners into capable, independent learners. Additionally, we can implement these sorts of AI fluency activities into the classroom. Indeed, an occasional level 3 activity with supervision and chat logs, does help teach AI fluency. An assignment to generate an AI essay and then grade that essay based on a rubric would be one excellent way to teach both the limitations to AI and allow the students to approach the essay writing process from a new direction. But, ultimately, if we want the student to learn how to write an essay, they must actually write an essay, and that’s not something we can thrust upon the students without first slowly giving them the tools, knowledge, and responsibility to do so.

title: How to implement AI assignments in the classroom
text: In this post we examined some guidelines for deciding how much AI usage is appropriate for students at different levels, but we provide no rules for actually implementing AI effectively. In particular, once we start allowing the AI and the student to interact directly, we open up a huge range of outcomes that we have limited control over. Unfortunately, many of these outcomes are bad, and so we must take care in how such AI assignments are implemented. To that end, I propose some guidelines to help keep things on track, and ensure that the student experience matches what you had in mind.

title: How to implement AI assignments in the classroom
text:
Design Principles

Set clear expectations
Designing a good AI assignment isn’t ultimately different from designing a good non-AI assignment. In both cases, setting clear expectations for all parties is critical. In the AI case, it’s even more important, since the AI is another entity that needs to have clear expectations for its role in the assignment, and its role in the assigment must be crystal clear. I recommend included an orientation document as part of the packet of documents that is uploaded to the AI, as shown in my statistics report trainer. For each stage of the project, along with the student-specific work, the AI receives an orientation.md file that outlines the overall project, which stage of the project is currently active, the specific actions the AI and the student should take during this stage, the desired outcome and deliverables of this stage, and the boundaries of permissible behavior for both the AI and the student. This is not a foolproof way of forcing the AI to act within the bounds you want to set for the assignment, but it goes a long way to priming the AI to create the right learning experience.
Similarly, the expectations should be equally clear for the student as well. This might take the form of a student brief, as included in the aforementioned statistics report trainer, or some other form, but the instructions should be clear for the student as well. You might even considering an in-class activity walking through an example assignment together, where you play the role of a student participating in the assignment. If practical, you can even include the chat log of the walkthrough as part of the assignment instructions, so it’s clear at each moment how the student should be engaging with the project.


Use AI as little as possible
This may seem somewhat contradictory given the general tone of the rest of this website, but bringing AI into an academic setting necessarily cedes control over part of the learning experience to that AI. If you can avoid doing this, then you should. This guidelines holds not just for the binary “should I use AI at all”, but how much AI is used. For example, with my statistics report trainer, that project began as a personal project to help me learn R. During that time, I used the AI haphazardly to generate experimental designs and datasets on the spot. When adapting that experience to a student assignment as presented in the portfolio piece, that level of AI usage became unacceptably prone to subtle errors, so instead of having the AI generate designs and data on the spot, we restrict it to pre-made and vetted datasets generated using Python. While students can easily get practice problems directly from an AI, in my pharmacy calculation practice tool, I restricted all direct AI/student interaction. Instead, I worked with AI to generate a problem bank from worked templates along with Python to generate the solutions programmatically from problem input numbers. In both cases, I’m not blindly ceding responsibility for learning to the AI, but using AI in a limited way to develop a vetted question bank that I have full control over.


One chat, one task
When both designing and assigning a task that involves AI, it’s useful to get into the habit of switching instances often. As the chat history grows longer and longer, the initial context of the chat has less and less influence on the behavior of the AI. The well-crafted orientation document is useless if the AI forgets about it, and a tightly restricted AI learning experience can readily become a mess if those restrictions get lost in the shuffle. To keep the AI sharp and on-task, it’s important to start fresh from a new instance regularly. In the statistics trainer tool, for instance, I have an entire second set of orientation documents for the evaluation stage of the experience. Not only does this ensure that the AI stays on target, it also prevents earlier instances from inadvertantly revealing answers to the student. Every instance has only what it needs for each stage, and switching to a new instance is built into the expectations for the experience.

title: How to implement AI assignments in the classroom
text:
Oversight Principles

Trust, but verify
As AI is implemented more and more freely, as responsibility for learning is shifted from the instructor to the student, the temptation to use AI in unintended ways grows and grows. While you can prime the AI to redirect the student or set boundaries in the orientation document, this is not foolproof, and a determined student can find ways around any boundaries you care to set. One way this behavior can be mitigated, though, is through oversight of the student’s interactions with the AI. For example, we might require the chat logs for a given AI assignment to be turned in alongside the assignment.


Avoid rogue AI
Whenever possible, the AI should not be an independent source of truth. It’s all too easy for an AI to get fixated on the wrong thing, miss important context, or just make stuff up. Obviously, we want to avoid that in our learning experiences. There’s not a foolproof way to do this, but we can stack the deck on our favor by providing a source of truth and instructing the AI to use only this source. We might include excerpts from textbooks or lecture notes in our uploaded material for an assignment, or we might pre-generate a question and solution bank and have the AI refer to that.


Fully test on a new instance
Lastly, we want to make sure anything we’re releasing to students has been thoroughly tested, and the principles for this testing are very similar to the principles we would use for proofreading, editing, or testing in other contexts as well. It’s always useful to get another set of eyes to catch things you might miss, and this holds true for AI. As an instance of AI continues to do things, it’s adding more and more text to its local context. Much like a human, it will solve problems, gain new insight, and create assumptions that another instance of AI will not have. Even giving another instance the full text of that entire history will not recreate the internal model of the previous instance. Then, it is critical that you use fresh instances to rigorously test your learning experience, tweak your orientation documents, and ensure that the student’s experience matches your plan.
This idea holds for using an AI to sanity check work. For example, if you want AI to do a pass of a question bank to identify potential errors, it’s much better to use a separate instance from the creation instance. You might even consider using an entirely different model to do this testing.

title: Daily Practice App for Pharmacutical Calculations
text:
Students in pharmacy school face unique challenges with pharmaceutical calculations. One problem in particular is the need for long-term retention of the material for boards. Pharmacy programs tend to be four year programs with the first three years being didactic and the final year being clinical rotations. Pharmaceutical calculations are often introduced in the first year, but then there’s a gap of three or more years before that material is required for board exams. To prepare students, pharmacy programs will commonly have cumulative review checkpoints throughout their curriculum to ensure that a student has retained (or recrammed) a basic level of understanding of pharmaceutical calculations. For example, a calculation refresher class during the third year and a board review program in the fourth year.
In spite of these refreshers, students often struggle with retention of the pharmaceutical calculation strategies. In other areas, such as the Top 300 drugs, students can rely on proven, spaced-repetition programs (such as Anki) to aid in retaining this sort of information, but no easy spaced-repetition program exists for pharmaceutical calculations. This program is an attempt to fill that gap.

text:
Design rationale
The core of this program is a practice problem bank combined with an Anki-inspired scheduler. Using Claude Opus 5.5, practice problem templates were generated for each topic subdivided by solution process (called skills in the program). Practice problems were generated using random input numbers according to realistic ranges for their problem, and then solutions were generated using custom python programs to ensure accuracy.
When a student first opens the program, they’re asked to select from a list of topics to build their deck. More topics can be added to their deck later, which allows students studying for review or board prep to select all topics, and students using the program alongside a course can slowly add new topics as they go. The student also selects a desired number of problems per day, with a recommended amount typically being three or four problems. This is an intentional change to the Anki design, where missing a day can lead to the load for the next day being unreasonably large. Here, the load is kept to a fixed amount with an optional catch-up mode that can give the student up to 50% additional problems if they have outstanding skills due.
This program uses a simplified version of the Anki FSRS algorithm to schedule problems based on the expected likelihood of a student getting that particular skill correct. The algorithm uses a statistic called “stability” to schedule each skill. Stability is roughly defined as the number of days after seeing the skill that it takes for a student to fall to a 90% expected probability of successfully solving the skill. Once a skill falls to its 90% solve probability, it becomes due, and the algorithm will start trying to show that skill again.
The program updates stability based on both whether a student got the latest instance of that skill correct or not, as well as an Anki-inspired difficulty rating for that problem. If a student gets a question wrong, they’re asked if they missed the problem due to an obvious mistake (slip) or if they were stuck on the problem altogether. If a student gets a problem correct, they’re asked to rate the problem as either hard, good, or easy. This rating gives a multiplier to stability, causing stability to shrink or grow by different amounts.
In addition, worked solutions for each problem are provided. These solutions were also generated by Claude Opus 5.5 from solution templates developed by the author. Solutions can be viewed both before an answer is given and after with an early peek counted as a stuck question.
Altogether, this app is designed to keep the student’s cognitive load to an absolute minimum while still providing them with an interleaved, spaced repetition practice regimen. The student never has to search for practice problems, try to keep track of which skills need attention, or worry about looking up solutions. The student is given a personalized study regimen that fits their schedule and adapts as they grow, while only requiring a ~15 minute time investment every day they choose to study.

How AI was used
This project fell under a level 1 AI-assisted educational project, where the focus is on keeping AI involvement separate from the student experience. AI was used heavily in the question bank development and app coding. To ensure a high-quality question bank that fully covered the different calculations encountered by pharmacy students, a list of topics was written by the author. Then, for each topic, they were divided into skills based on the solution processes needed, referencing this calculations flowchart. For example, dilution and evaporation problems, while seemingly divided into two separate skills, actually follow nearly identical solution processes: solve a single variable equation for c_1 v_1 = c_2 v_2. Single-solution problems, on the other hand, were divided into three skills depending on if the student needed to identify concentration, amount of drug or total, or amount of solvent. Once the list of topics and skills was finalized, Claude Opus 5.5 was utilized to create roughly a dozen different problem templates per skill (changing the relevant drug or scenario). Then, for each template, five or six individual problems were generated to make up the problem bank.
To avoid AI-hallucinations, the individual problems used randomly generated input numbers generated by the AI to fall within reasonable expected ranges for the template’s drugs. The solutions to each problem, on the other hand, were generated programmatically from the input numbers using an AI-created Python program for each problem template. I then checked an examplar from each skill to check for any obvious errors. To further ensure the accuracy of problems, I engage in a daily routine of solving my own practice questions to identify bad questions or otherwise check the quality of the app.
Claude was also used to generate the worked solutions for each problem template. For each skill, an examplar solution was developed by Claude, based off of example solution processes I developed. These exemplars were then presented to me and checked for accuracy and style, and the style point in particular is where Claude seems to struggle the most. I would often make changes to have the solution processes flow better or focus only on the key points of the problem. title: Statistical Analysis Trainer
text:
Design rationale
For new students learning game design and attempting to create their own games, a common adage is “finish a game as quickly as possible”. It’s important for a new learner to see all stages of game design to gain a better understanding of game design as a holistic process. When learning a new statistical langauge and learning how to perform a statistical analysis, it is useful to use a similar approach, and this trainer is an attempt to build a workflow to get a student producing a minimum viable statistical analysis in their language of choice as quickly as possible and then checking the quality of that analysis against a vetted reference analysis.
Following principles of good design, we divide the workflow into two distinct stages, a planning stage and a reveal stage. Each stage begins with a new AI instance and has its own dedicated AI orientation documents and student briefs. The planning stage AI recieves its orientation document, the experimental design description, and the dataset. The reveal stage AI receives its own orientation document, the experimental design description, the dataset, as well as the solution key and the student’s statistical report. This way each stage is kept independent, and the planning AI is unable to easily give away any information to the student. This was a common problem I encountered in my initial experiments with this workflow: an AI would be instructed not to reveal any information about the intended analysis, and then do something like name the dataset “logistic-regression-data.csv”.
While initial experimentation had the AI generate the datasets and the experimental design descriptions on the spot (and it did surprisingly well at this), we found that this had the potential for subtle errors. For example, one analysis examined generated data about patient recovery after different types of heart surgeries. In this scenario, the variable length_of_stay measured the number of days post-surgery the patient stayed at the hospital, and this variable was intended to be correlated to the type of surgery. When the data was generated, however, this correlation was not implemented, which lead to a difference between the intended analysis and the actual data. Since these sorts of errors are hidden in sets of data, they can be difficult to spot, and so we avoid this problem by pre-generating and testing experimental design descriptions and datasets to ensure accuracy.
Each pregenerated dataset comes with a chance of having a potential complication in the data that the student must account for. The current list of possible complications is violations of assumptions, underpowered true effects, aliased variables, outcome-dependent variables, post-treatment variables, confounding variables, and unbalanced groups. This is an intential design choice to force the student to diligently check their assumptions and variables. Currently, zero to one complications are chosen when generating each dataset, and these complications are checked to make sure they measurably distort the outcomes of the analysis if not correctly handled with the exception of underpowered true effects. For underpowered true effects, these complications are not meant to distort the analysis, but to impress on the student that even a correct analysis can miss true effects due to random chance in sampling or underpowered experiments.

This is an exercise in using an AI workflow to engage in statistical analysis of a pre-generated experiment and dataset. Your role will be to review the experimental design description and dataset, decide on the appropriate statistical tests to run, analyze the data using your statistical software of choice, and then write up a brief report presenting your statistical analysis. The goal is to give you a beginning-to-end experience of doing a statistical analysis. This exercise works in two stages, with two sets of folders marked stage 1 and stage 2. In stage 1, you will upload the content of the stage 1 folder (ai-orientation-1.md, data.csv, experimental-description.md) to your AI of choice. The AI’s role is to provide with assistance running the tests and writing the report. The AI should help with using the statistical software, enabling you to run your chosen tests, interpreting errors and outputs. The AI should not help you with making decisions about which methods are appropriate, analyzing the dataset, or hinting towards the correct answer.
For stage 1, you will upload the appropriate documents and then review experimental-description.md and data.csv. From the design description, you will choose the appropriate method to analyze the data. You will then decide on which variables, if any, should be excluded from the analysis for design reasons. You will then check that the relevant statistical assumptions are met for your chosen method, note any existing complications in the data, fit the model using your statistical software of choice, and then write the report. The report should include

the design,
your chosen method of analysis with justification,
a decision to include or exclude for each variable with justification,
checks of the relevant assumptions for your chosen method,
results with effect sizes and confidence intervals, and
interpretation of those results with respect to the initial experimental design.

Once the report is written, you should upload the report and the contents of the stage 2 folder (solution-key.md, experimental-description.md, data.csv, ai-orientation-2.md) to a new AI instance. This is to avoid prior discussion with the first AI instance from influencing the analysis of your report. Once the report is uploaded, the new AI instance will evaluate your report against the solution key. The AI will provide some hints as to errors in the analysis, if any exist, and then give you one opportunity to find and revise the errors. If revision is necessary, make the revisions and reupload the revised report. The AI will then reveal the contents of the solution key, included which variables should have been excluded, what complications existed in the data (if any), the results of the statistical tests and model fitting, and the intended interpretation of those results.
This project is expected to be completed in 20-60 minutes depending on your fluency with statistical analysis and your chosen statistical software. While you have access to the solution key in order to upload it to the AI in stage 2, you are strongly encouraged not to look at it before it is revealed at the end of the exercise.




You are an AI assistant helping a student learn to write a minimal statistical analysis. The goal is for a student to be presented with a short experimental design description and a dataset and then write up a complete statistical analysis on the dataset. This dataset may have complications included, such as violations of assumptions, underpowered true effects, aliased variables, outcome-dependent variables, post-treatment variables, confounding variables, and unbalanced groups, so the student will have to check for common complications to ensure their analysis is correct. Your role is to assist the student in this learning experiment without giving away hints to the true solution. Once the report is written, the student will move on to stage 2. For stage 2, the student will upload their report to a new, fresh AI instance, along with a pre-generated key and a new orientation document. This other AI instance will engage in a revision round with the student and then present the answer key, any included complications, and the true effects used to generate the data. The entire analysis is intended to be completed in a single sitting of approximately 20-60 minutes, depending on the student’s familiarity with their software of choice and the statistical analysis. your chosen method of analysis with justification,
a decision to include or exclude for each variable with justification,
checks of the relevant assumptions for your chosen method,
results with effect sizes and confidence intervals, and
interpretation of those results with respect to the initial experimental design.

The student might be working on this independently or as part of a course on statistics. The student might be generally unfamiliar with their statistical software of choice or with statistics more broadly. Your role is to assist the student with syntax and functions, error messages and debugging, how to run a method that the student has chosen, and explaining what a piece of output means if asked. You should not choose the method, choose which variables to include or exclude, write the report’s prose or interpretation, or run the analysis for them.
You have not been given an answer key. This is an intentional design choice to prevent you from inadvertently providing this information to the student. Your instinct is right on both counts, and this is a well-studied question.
What randomization actually guarantees
Randomization makes covariates independent of treatment in expectation, over all possible randomizations. Any single realized allocation can be imbalanced by chance. The key point is that this chance imbalance is already accounted for in the inference: p-values and confidence intervals are calibrated over the randomization distribution, which includes the unlucky allocations. So “we had some imbalance by chance, and we proceed” is the textbook-correct stance, not biting a bullet.
Why significance-testing balance is discouraged
Many trials used to report p-values comparing baseline characteristics between arms. CONSORT and most methodologists now advise against this. If randomization was done properly, the null hypothesis is true by construction, so any “significant” difference is by definition a false positive. A descriptive table (means, SDs, percentages) is the recommended way to report balance. Then you judge whether any difference is large enough to matter clinically, not statistically.
How imbalance is handled in practice

Pre-specified covariate adjustment. This is the main tool, and it’s what ANCOVA does. Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates corrects for chance imbalance in them and usually tightens the confidence interval. The important part is choosing covariates in advance, based on prior knowledge of what predicts the outcome, not after looking at which ones came out imbalanced. Choosing adjustment variables based on observed imbalance opens the door to analytic flexibility.
Design-stage fixes, done before allocation:

Stratified (blocked) randomization: randomize separately within strata, e.g., diabetic and non-diabetic patients, so those groups are balanced by design.
Minimization: each new patient is allocated, partly at random, to whichever arm best preserves balance across several factors. It’s common in smaller trials.
Rerandomization: your “hacky” idea is actually a legitimate method (Morgan & Rubin, 2012), if the acceptance rule is specified in advance (e.g., “redraw until the Mahalanobis distance between arms is below threshold a”), and the analysis accounts for the restricted set of allowable allocations. What’s hacky is doing it ad hoc and then analyzing as if it were simple randomization.


Summary: randomize once (or with a pre-specified restriction), report balance descriptively, adjust for pre-specified prognostic covariates, and don’t let the observed balance drive the analysis choices.

Big messes can be linear. Linearity is about the shape of the average relationship, not how tightly the points cluster around it.

Scatter (noise) is about the strength of the relationship. A lot of spread just means the covariate explains a modest share of the variation, which is fine for ANCOVA.

title: Statistical Analysis Trainer
text:
How AI was used
In the design process, AI was used primarily to generate the datasets, experimental design descriptions, and review keys in the problem bank. Claude Opus 5.5 was asked to create a python program to generate data with a number of possible complications to the data as well as generating the text of a plausible associated experimental design. Claude was then used to check the dataset and ensure that any complication in the data are detectable. Then, Claude was used the generate a review key. The review key contains intended methods of analysis for the data based on the experimental design, a summary of the data, any included complications to the data and how that complication can influence the analysis if not handled, and the expected findings. This collection of experiments, datasets, and keys was then checked by a fresh instance of Claude Opus 5.5 to ensure accuracy.

Reflection
Overall, I’m happy with this project. I think it’s a good workflow for getting started with a new software while practicing a full cycle of statistical analysis. For taking this project to the next level, I think it would be interesting to make a larger framework around this project that can persistently track a student’s progress and adapt to their growth. This current project might be considered the easiest and most scaffolded, and we might increase the difficulty by adding multiple complications to the data, making the data messier and requiring cleaning as a first step, or by further restricting how much help the AI is allowed to give.
This might look like creating a webpage, similar to the pharmacy calculations practice app, that tracks the student’s uploaded projects and “grades” each one, increasing the difficulty of future tasks as appropriate. This has a number of potential issues in implementation, particularly with how AI would be implemented into the web page itself and how usage would be kept reasonable.
Another possibility for implementing a persistent memory of student progress would be simply to have the AI revise and output a document at the end of each stage 2 that records each experiment and summarizes any issues with the student’s report. The AI orientation documents could be revised to reference this progress document. This potential approach seems promising for keeping the project lightweight and portable, but we do run into some potential issues for how the student is actually given their harder datasets. It might be necessary to have the stage 1 AI generate the data itself from the Python program directly. This loses out on the testing and partitioned stages, though, so it’s less than ideal. It might necessitate a three stage workflow, where the initial stage is to have the AI generate and check the data, and then move that into the usual stage 1 and stage 2 workflow.
